title: Man is shot dead, officer hit in park; Witnesses tell of upset person walking in ravine Police open fire when he lunges with knife
article: A man was shot dead yesterday by police in a beautiful and normally tranquil park near Edwards Gardens.

Witnesses said the man appeared to be emotionally disturbed and was carrying a knife. Police sources said three officers fired their guns when he allegedly lunged at them in Wilket Creek Park, a lush ravine area west of Leslie St. and between Eglinton and Lawrence Aves.
Three officers were injured, including one who was treated for a gunshot wound in his leg inflicted by a police bullet.
The coroner's office is trying to determine the identity of the deceased man, who was described as black and in his 20s.

Witnesses and police sources told the Star that police from nearby 33 Division were called to the area shortly after noon, after a man armed with a knife was seen walking along Lawrence Ave. E. The three officers searched for the man in nearby Edwards Gardens, which is connected to Wilket Creek Park by a cycling and walking path.
When they caught up with him in Wilket Creek, police sources said, he was swinging an electrical cord in one hand and the officers tried to calm him down.
According to police sources, the man started to run and the officers followed.
He allegedly lunged at them with a knife when they caught up with him.
All three officers fired their guns, sources said.
"Things get crazy when people are trying to stab and kill you," police lawyer Gary Clewley said yesterday outside Sunnybrook hospital, where one officer was being treated for a minor "flesh wound."
Police are investigating exactly how the officer was shot.
Ontario's Deputy Chief Coroner Dr. Jim Cairns said last night that the slain man had no identification with him; his fingerprints were taken to try to determine his identity and notify his family.
The shooting near Edwards Gardens - a popular site for family picnics and as a backdrop for wedding day pictures - shocked visitors to the area.

Salima Hadibhai and Shakeel Ladha had been having their engagement pictures taken near a stream and beds of vibrant flowers in Edward Gardens yesterday when they saw a man enter the park. They said he was shirtless, his pants appeared to be falling off his hips, and he was visibly upset and muttering. They watched as he walked toward a forested area.
A few minutes later they heard sirens and saw three officers.
"We pointed to the area where he went, saying he went this way," said the couple's photographer, Zahir Hirji, adding they hadn't called police but assumed the officers were looking for the same man.
After the shooting, police used yellow tape to cordon off an area in the park near a footbridge. Cyclists and pedestrians were turned away. The area had been reopened by nightfall.
"I run down there all the time and you wouldn't expect this kind of thing to happen here," said 29-year-old Carla Edmiston as she left the park on her bike.
Paul Liang was hiking on one of the paths when he saw paramedics trying to revive a man.
"I thought somebody could have hurt himself; you know, maybe falling off a bike or something," 35-year-old Liang said yesterday when told about the shooting.
Fire department officials escorted a visibly shaken man from the scene. He was wearing shorts and carrying his T-shirt in his hands.
He told one of the firefighters there was blood on the shirt; he was given medical attention and driven away in a fire truck.

Police spokesperson Jim Muscat could not confirm reports that the man was a doctor, but said witnesses at the scene who "provided first aid may have had medical training." Muscat said the officer who was shot is expected to "make a full recovery."

Mark Pugash, the Toronto police force's director of corporate communications, refused to comment on the shooting, saying the province's Special Investigations Unit, which is called in whenever someone is injured or killed and police are involved, could comment.

It's not known if the slain man was mentally ill. But author and mental health advocate Pat Capponi said yesterday that police should be trained to react calmly in a situation where someone is armed and possibly mentally ill.
"If police had sufficient training on how to cool down this situation it wouldn't lead to three guys shooting at one guy with a knife," she said yesterday.
"Training trumps fear. Training trumps panic."

In the past few months, the SIU has been called to investigate the death of Quincy Cancar, who shot himself in the head as police arrived on the scene on Yonge St., near Wellesley St. Sources have told the Star that officers ordered him to drop a weapon, but 27- year-old Cancar refused, shouting "you're not going to take me."

On May 21, an undercover officer fatally shot 17-year-old Jeffrey Reodica after a confrontation in a quiet Scarborough neighbourhood around the corner from the bungalow where the teenager lived. Reodica died after being taken off life support at Sunnybrook hospital three days after the shooting.

In January, the issue of the police use of force in dealing with mentally ill suspects arose with the fatal shooting of 63-year-old Antonio Bellon. The SIU cleared the officer involved after its investigation, but mental health advocates demanded better training for officers.
Much has changed over the years in the way police deal with those people emergency dispatchers used to call "MI's" (mentally ill) and now call "EDPs" (emotionally disturbed person).

Spurred by the deaths of Edmond Yu, Lester Donaldson, Dominic Sabatino, Wayne Williams, Tommy Barnett and others with a psychiatric history who have died in confrontations with police, officers now undergo mandatory training at the Ontario Police College to learn how to deal with calls involving people with mental illness.

There was also created what is known as the Mobile Crisis Intervention Team, known to dispatchers as "CIT-O1," which consists of a police officer not in uniform and a mental-health nurse. But that unit only works Monday to Friday and in cases where someone is armed it would likely not be called in.

Police protocol requires that the force's highly trained Emergency Task Force be contacted whenever there is a call involving a person who is mentally ill. ETF trucks were at the entrance of the park yesterday but it's unclear when they arrived. Witnesses said there were only three uniformed officers at the scene of the shooting.
"It's too bad the ETF wasn't there," said Capponi, noting the unit's impressive record of defusing tense situations without force. "
